L4@P0: Spatial Variation of Supply Water Quality Parameters Across Dhaka City
L5@P0: M. E. H. Emon1*, K. Fatema2, A.S Akib2, M.H Nayeem2, J. Akter2 & M.S.S. Chowdhury1
L6@P0: 1 Lecturer, Department of Civil Engineering, Prime University, Bangladesh (emrankuet38@gmail.com and
L7@P0: shadmansakibchowdhury@gmail.com )
L8@P0: 2 Under-graduate Student, Department of Civil Engineering, Prime University, Bangladesh
L9@P0: (im.kanizfatema2004@gmail.com, akib34613@gmail.com, nayeemh050@gmail.com, and

L11@P0: Abstract
L12@P0: In urban areas like Dhaka, point-of-use water quality monitoring is often overlooked due to the high cost and
L13@P0: difficulty of widespread sampling. This study evaluates the spatial variation of key water quality parameters
L14@P0: hardness, sulfate, chloride, and nitrate ions in Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (DWASA) supplied
L15@P0: tap water across 13 locations in Dhaka city. Water samples were collected directly from household taps to
L16@P0: represent actual consumer exposure. The analysis revealed notable variations among locations. Amin Bazar
L17@P0: recorded the highest water hardness (300 mg/l), while Kuril showed the lowest (33 mg/l). Chloride levels were
L18@P0: highest in Amin Bazar (233.93 mg/l) and lowest in Rampura (39.99 mg/l). Sulfate ion concentrations were
L19@P0: mostly below 20 mg/l, except in Amin Bazar (90 mg/l) and Kamlapur (42 mg/l), indicating local anomalies.
L20@P0: Nitrate was detected only in Tongi (15 mg/l) and Amin Bazar (20 mg/l), with all other locations showing 0 mg/l.
L21@P0: These variations suggest the influence of pipe age, source water quality, and potential infrastructure issues. The
L22@P0: study emphasizes the need for regular and localized monitoring to help identify areas with deteriorating pipelines
L23@P0: and support Water Supply Authorities (WSA) in prioritizing maintenance efforts effectively.
L24@P0: Keywords: Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage Authority (DWASA), Water Supply Authorities (WSA)
L25@P0: 1 Introduction
L26@P0: Access to clean and safe drinking water is essential for human health, well-being, and sustainable urban
L27@P0: development (E. Cicia et al., 2010; Crase et al., 2005). In densely populated cities like Dhaka, the capital of
L28@P0: Bangladesh, the provision of safe and reliable tap water has become increasingly challenging due to rapid
L29@P0: urbanization, industrial expansion, population growth, and aging infrastructure (Cidu et al., 2010). With over
L30@P0: 10.28 million residents Dhaka faces mounting pressure on its municipal water supply system, resulting in
L31@P0: widespread concerns over water safety and quality. (Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics [BBS], 2022). Water
L32@P0: contamination in urban settings can stem from several factors, including microbial pathogens, heavy metals, and
L33@P0: chemical pollutants, often aggravated by poor water treatment practices, outdated pipelines, and illegal industrial
L34@P0: discharges (Allaire et al., 2018; Trueman et al., 2019). Numerous studies have shown that insufficient oversight
L35@P0: and lack of maintenance in water distribution systems can lead to significant deterioration in tap water quality,
L36@P0: heightening the risk of gastrointestinal illnesses, heavy metal toxicity, and other waterborne diseases (Cidu et al.,
L37@P0: 2010; Kachel et al., 2007; Zivin et al., 2011). Furthermore, public perception plays a critical role in water use
L38@P0: behavior. Consumers often assess water quality based not only on objective safety parameters but also on
L39@P0: sensory attributes like taste, odor, and color (Um et al., 2002; McDonald and Rundle, 2006). In Dhaka, this disconnect between perceived and actual water quality has led to a growing dependence on bottled water and home
L40@P0: filtration systems, reflecting broader issues of trust in public water utilities and regulatory enforcement (Crase,
L41@P0: 2007; Zivin et al., 2011). Globally, the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) emphasize the
L42@P0: importance of achieving universal and equitable access to safe and affordable drinking water by 2030 (UN,
L43@P0: 2015). However, in many low- and middle-income urban centers like Dhaka, progress remains constrained by
L44@P0: infrastructural, financial, and governance limitations. This study aims to evaluate both the objective and
L45@P0: perceived quality of tap water in selected areas of Dhaka city. It compares municipal and bottled water sources in
L46@P0: light of national and international drinking water standards, while also examining public perception through
L47@P0: household-level surveys. The findings are intended to inform policy strategies for improving water quality
L48@P0: governance, enhancing infrastructure, and protecting public health in rapidly urbanizing environment.
L49@P0: 2.Methodology
L50@P0: 2.1 Location Selection and collection of water Sample
L51@P0: According to the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics’ 2022 Census and official metropolitan records, Dhaka North
L52@P0-1: City Corporation covers approximately 196.22 km², and Dhaka South City Corporation covers approximately M. E. H. Emon, K. Fatema, A.S Akib, M.H Nayeem, J. Akter & M.S.S. Chowdhury

L54@P1: 1630
L55@P1: 109.24 km², resulting in a combined administrative area of about 305.46 km² (Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics
L56@P1: [BBS], 2022). This makes Dhaka the largest city in Bangladesh by area. The Dhaka Water Supply and Sewerage
L57@P1: Authority (DWASA) is responsible for supplying water throughout the entire city. To assess selected water
L58@P1: quality parameters, this study identified 13 locations across Dhaka City, encompassing both the North and South
L59@P1: city corporations. These locations are illustrated in Figure 1. For the purpose of this study, household tap water
L60@P1: samples were collected from each of the selected locations, as shown in Figure 2.
L61@P1: 2.2 Determination of Water Quality Parameters
L62@P1: 2.2.1 Chloride Ion (Cl-)
L63@P1: 2.2.1.1 Principle of the Test (Mohr’s Method)
L64@P1: After collecting the water samples, they were transported to the laboratory and analyzed within 24 hours to
L65@P1: ensure accuracy in water quality assessment. For the determination of chloride ions, a titration method using a
L66@P1: standard silver nitrate (AgNO₃) solution was employed. The 0.0141 N AgNO₃ solution was prepared by
L67@P1: accurately dissolving 2.395 g of silver nitrate in distilled water, transferring it to a 1-liter volumetric flask, and
L68@P1: diluting it to the mark, as depicted in Fig. 3a. Since AgNO₃ is photosensitive, it was stored in a dark bottle. A 5%
L69@P1: potassium chromate (K₂CrO₄) solution was used as an indicator, prepared by dissolving 5g of K₂CrO₄ in 100 mL
L70@P1: of distilled water, then filtered and stored in a sealed container as depicted in Fig. 3b. A standard sodium chloride
L71@P1: (NaCl) solution of 0.0141 N was also prepared by dissolving 0.824 g of pre-dried NaCl (at 105°C) in distilled
L72@P1: water and diluting it to 1 liter as depicted in Fig. 3c. For the titration, 25 mL of the water sample was pipetted
L73@P1: into a clean conical flask, followed by the addition of 1 mL of potassium chromate indicator. The sample was
L74@P1: titrated with the silver nitrate solution until the appearance of a permanent red-brown color indicated the
L75@P1: endpoint, as depicted in Fig. 3d, resulting from the formation of silver chromate (Ag₂CrO₄) after all chloride ions
L76@P1: had reacted with silver to form silver chloride (AgCl). The volume of AgNO₃ consumed was recorded for
L77@P1: chloride concentration calculation. The concentration of chloride ions (in mg/L) was calculated using the
L78@P1: following formula:
L79@P1: Chloride (mg/L) = (V×N×35.45×1000)/Sample Volume (1)
L80@P1: Where, V = volume of AgNO₃ used (mL), N = normality of AgNO₃, and 35.45 = molar mass of Cl⁻
L81@P1: 2.2.2 Hardness Determination
L82@P1: For total hardness determination, a clean 5 mL plastic beaker was rinsed and filled with the water sample. Five
L83@P1: drops of hardness buffer and one drop of Calmagite indicator were added through the cap port, and the solution
L84@P1: was gently swirled. A red-violet color indicated the presence of hardness ions. Using a titration syringe, EDTA
L85@P1: titrant (HI 3812-0) was added dropwise with swirling after each drop. The color shifted from red-violet to purple,
L86@P1: and finally to blue as shown in Fig. 4, marking the endpoint. The volume of EDTA used was recorded and
L87@P1: multiplied by 300 to express total hardness in mg/L as CaCO₃.
L88@P1: 2.2.3 Sulfate Ion Determination
L89@P1: Sulfate concentration in the water sample was determined using a visual turbidity-based method. A plastic vessel
L90@P1: was filled with 50 mL of the sample, followed by the addition of one packet of HI 38000A-0 Sulfate Reagent,
L91@P1: and the solution was gently swirled to ensure complete dissolution. Two drops of Complexing Agent and two
L92@P1: spoons of HI 38000B-0 Reagent were then added with thorough mixing. The mixture was allowed to stand
L93@P1: undisturbed for 5 minutes to allow for full reaction development. The test tube was placed on a white surface,
L94@P1: and the sample was added dropwise using a plastic pipette until the black spot at the bottom was no longer
L95@P1: visible as depicted in Fig. 5A and Fig. 5B. The sulfate concentration was determined by reading the liquid level
L96@P1: in the tube, expressed in mg/L (ppm).
L97@P1: 2.2.4 Nitrate Ion Determination
L98@P1: Nitrate concentration in the water sample was determined using a colorimetric method. A plastic vessel was
L99@P1: rinsed and filled with 10 mL of the sample, after which one packet of HI 3834-0 reagent was added. The vessel
L100@P1: was capped and shaken until the reagent fully dissolved. The resulting solution was transferred into a color
L101@P1: comparator cube and left undisturbed for 4 minutes to allow complete color development. The final color was
L102@P1: then visually compared with a standard reference scale as shown in Fig. 6, and the corresponding concentration
L103@P1: was recorded in mg/L (ppm). A noticeable color change in the sample collected from Amin Bazar confirmed the
L104@P1: presence of nitrate in the water. This colorimetric response confirms that nitrate contamination is present at
L105@P1-2: measurable levels in the Amin Bazar water sample.M. E. H. Emon, K. Fatema, A.S Akib, M.H Nayeem, J. Akter & M.S.S. Chowdhury

L117@P2: 3. Result and Discussion
L118@P2: 3.1 Sulfate
L119@P2: The measured sulfate concentrations in all the selected areas of Dhaka city ranged from <20 mg/L to a maximum
L120@P2: of 90 mg/L in Amin Bazar as shown in Table 2, which is well below both the Bangladesh and WHO guideline
L121@P2: value of 400 mg/L as shown in Table 3. According to standard classification, sulfate levels below 250 mg/L are
L122@P2: considered safe for drinking and general domestic use. Most locations such as Jasim Uddin, Dhanmondi,
L123@P2: Mohammadpur, Rampura, and others showed sulfate concentrations below 20 mg/L, indicating very low sulfate
L124@P2: presence and suggesting minimal anthropogenic influence or effective protection of groundwater sources.
L125@P2: Moderately higher values were observed in Mirpur (23 mg/L), Motijheel (27 mg/L), Kamlapur (42 mg/L), and
L126@P2: Gabtoli (27 mg/L), likely due to moderate urban runoff and sewage contamination. Amin Bazar exhibited the
L127@P2: highest sulfate level (90 mg/L), probably linked to landfill leachate, poor sanitation, and open dumping. Though
L128@P2: all observed values fall within safe limits, elevated sulfate concentrations even below the threshold can
L129@P2: contribute to scale buildup in pipelines, reduce the efficiency of water heaters, and slightly alter taste, affecting

L187@P3: 3.2 Hardness
L188@P3: The measured hardness of water samples from Dhaka city ranged from 33 mg/L at Kuril, classified as slightly
L189@P3: hard according to WHO guidelines, to 300 mg/L at Amin Bazar, which falls into the very hard category as
L190@P3: depicted in Table 1. Specifically, Kuril (33 mg/L) was slightly hard, Jasim Uddin (45 mg/L) and Motijheel (51
L191@P3: mg/L) were also in the slightly hard range, while Abdullahpur (60 mg/L) and Kochu Khet (90 mg/L) were
L192@P3: classified as moderately hard as shown in Fig. 7. Locations like Tongi (126 mg/L), Mirpur (144 mg/L), Rampura
L193@P3: (150 mg/L), Dhanmondi (105 mg/L), and Mohammadpur (150 mg/L) were in the hard category, while Gabtoli
L194@P3: (195 mg/L) and Amin Bazar (300 mg/L) were in the very hard category. According to Bangladesh standards
L195@P3: (150–500 mg/L) and WHO’s aesthetic limit (200 mg/L), most samples were within acceptable limits, but Amin
L196@P3-4: Bazar (300 mg/L) exceeded the WHO guideline, indicating potential problems such as scaling in plumbing M. E. H. Emon, K. Fatema, A.S Akib, M.H Nayeem, J. Akter & M.S.S. Chowdhury

L203@P4: 3.3 Chloride Ion (Cl-)
L204@P4: The chloride ion (Cl⁻) concentrations measured across various locations ranged from 39.99 mg/L to 233.93 mg/L
L205@P4: as shown in Table 2. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), the guideline value for chloride in
L206@P4: drinking water is 250 mg/L, primarily for aesthetic reasons such as taste and corrosivity. Bangladesh standards
L207@P4: (BSTI) also recommend a range of 150–600 mg/L as depicted in Table 3. While all tested sites were within the
L208@P4: permissible limits, Amin Bazar (233.93 mg/L) and Gabtoli (215.93 mg/L) were close to the upper boundary,
L209@P4: indicating potential future risks. High chloride levels can corrode metal components in pumps, pipelines, and
L210@P4: plumbing systems, leading to reduced equipment lifespan, leaks, and increased maintenance costs. Corrosion
L211@P4: may also cause toxic metals like lead or iron to leach into the water supply, posing health risks. Although
L212@P4: chloride itself is not harmful at these levels, the associated effects on infrastructure and secondary contamination
L213@P4: are concerning. Areas like Mohammadpur and Kochukhet showed moderately high values and require regular
L214@P4: monitoring. In contrast, locations such as Rampura, Kuril, and Motijheel exhibited low chloride levels and pose
L215@P4: minimal risk. Preventive measures like using corrosion-resistant materials, regular testing, and public awareness
L216@P4: are recommended to ensure long-term water safety and infrastructure integrity.
L217@P4: 3.4 Nitrate (NO₃⁻) concentrations
L218@P4: Nitrate (NO₃⁻) concentrations in the sampled locations spanned 0 mg/L to 20 mg/L, with eleven sites including
L219@P4: Jasim Uddin, Abdullahpur, Kuril, Gabtoli, Mohammadpur, Mirpur, Kamalapur, Motijheel, Dhanmondi, Rampura
L220@P4: and Kochukhet showing no detectable nitrate, while Tongi registered about 15 mg/L and Amin Bazar about 20
L221@P4: mg/L as depicted in Table 2. These values are comfortably below the World Health Organization (WHO)
L222@P4: guideline of 10 mg/L and the Bangladesh drinking-water standard of 50 mg/L as shown in Table 3, yet the two
L223@P4: elevated sites warrant attention because nitrate can convert to nitrite in the body and impair oxygen transport,
L224@P4: triggering methemoglobinemia in infants and posing long-term risks such as thyroid dysfunction. Rising nitrate
L225@P4: often signals agricultural runoff, leaking sewage or aging plumbing that allows contaminated surface water to
L226@P4: infiltrate supply lines; if unchecked, it can overload treatment units, foul pumps and hasten biofilm growth in
L227@P4: distribution pipes. Consequently, Tongi and Amin Bazar should undergo more frequent monitoring, sourcetracking and possibly improvements to wastewater control and pipe integrity, while the other locations remain
L228@P4: low-risk provided routine surveillance and good agricultural and plumbing practices are maintained.
L229@P4: 4. Conclusion
L230@P4: The groundwater quality assessment conducted across various locations of Dhaka city indicates that while the
L231@P4: measured parameters including sulfate, hardness, chloride, and nitrate are within both the Bangladesh National
L232@P4: Standards and WHO guideline values, spatial variations suggest localized sources of contamination and differing
L233@P4: hydrogeological conditions. Amin Bazar consistently exhibited the highest concentrations for multiple
L234@P4: parameters, particularly sulfate (90 mg/L), hardness (300 mg/L), chloride (233.93 mg/L), and nitrate (20 mg/L),
L235@P4: pointing toward the influence of landfill leachate, poor sanitation infrastructure, and possible surface water
L236@P4: intrusion. In contrast, residential areas such as Dhanmondi, Mohammadpur, and Jasim Uddin recorded lower
L237@P4: contaminant levels, indicating relatively protected aquifers and effective groundwater abstraction practices.

L241@P5: Amin Bazar) suggests potential issues with scale buildup in pipelines, reduced soap efficiency, and long-term
L242@P5: infrastructure wear. Similarly, higher chloride values in Gabtoli and Amin Bazar may lead to corrosion of
L243@P5: plumbing systems, indirectly posing risks through metal leaching. Though nitrate concentrations remained within
L244@P5: safe limits, the slightly higher values in Amin Bazar and Tongi warrant attention, as they may indicate sewage
L245@P5: leakage or agricultural runoff. These findings emphasize the need for area-specific groundwater management,
L246@P5: regular quality monitoring, and improved urban waste disposal systems to safeguard the city's drinking water
L247@P5: supply. Continuous surveillance and appropriate mitigation strategies are essential to maintain water quality,
L248@P5: minimize public health risks, and ensure the longevity of DWASA’s distribution infrastructure.
